request.purpose: Αναζήτησε πηγές για τη Μήλο, το λιμάνι και τα αγκυροβόλιά της, τη ναυτική κίνηση και την πειρατική/κουρσάρικη παρουσία αποκλειστικά με χρονολογικό έλεγχο 1660–1680. Κατάγραψε ακριβείς παραπομπές και μη αναγνώσιμο υλικό.

findings.title: Η Ιστορια της Αφροδιτης της Μήλος / The Story of the Aphrodite of Milos
findings.creator: Gianni M. Chalkoutsaki
findings.description: A general history of the Aphrodite of Milos (Venus de Milo). The author wrote the book with Greek readers in mind. The author's stated purpose was to methodically compare accounts and eyewitness stories to find the truth about the discovery of the statue, and what happened to the statue subsequently. A quick history of the island of Milos, a small number of illustrations and two maps are included. A few pages are legible but slightly blurry in the gutters due to scanning. There is some Greek handwriting in a few spots (notes)?

findings.title: ON THE ROAD - A Coruna / Dakar
findings.creator: Sufus Hufus
findings.description: ON THE ROAD -  A Coru ña / Dakar So, I’m leaving A Coruña, a city placed on the top-west corner of Spain, Galicia department. Actually walking along the Fernando Suárez García avenue now, an avenue just in front of the sea, by the left side of the Orzán cove, that the Greco-Roman geographers designated as Portus Magnus Artabrorum. being the Artabri, I got to know, an ancient Gallaeci-Celtic tribe that used to dwell around this lands. And so, as I walk by the Paseo Maritimo, I’m actually contemplating the imposing masses of granite rocks that rise against the harshness of the sea. And, with very fresh winds blowing against my face, I actually pass by the “Miradoiro Fiestra ó Atlántico”, that lays just in front of three small islets, Illa Vendaval, Illa do Pé, and Illa Aguión. Further, I’m actually going around a small and sympathetic cove that form the Portiño harbor, also called “Porto de San Pedro de Visma”, being Visma the name of the neighborhood here, and well, as it goes, I’m now passing right on the side of the Miradoiro do Faroleiro (Lighthouse Keeper's viewpoint), following along the Punta do Burro (donkey's tip), soon reaching Suevos, a small hamlet that is part of the Arteixo municipality, named like this after the Suevi, a group of Germanic peoples that migrated from central Europe to this area during the “barbarian” invasions of the fifth century, I got to know. Then, after exchanging some impressions with the villagers I meet on the street, in front of houses with unpainted walls. I’m leaving this humble hamlet on the top of the hill, coming back to the seaside, already going along the “soap beach” or “Praia de Sabón”, getting close to Malpica, a place indicated as the starting point of the so-called “death coast”, known for its high cliffs and severe weather, located near the  Sisargas Islands , a notoriously dangerous, rocky spot where numerous ships have sunk… I got to know. And so, as I walk by this piece of coast, I pass by the Beo beach, the Seiruga beach, the Barizo beach, the Punta Nariga lighthouse, then going along a narrow dirt path through lush, low-lying vegetation, always by the sea, I end up reaching the Areia de Prata beach, plus the Niñóns and the Morro beach. Afterwards, as I come back to the road, I will pass Brantuas de Arriba, Casas da Espereira, Brantuas de Abaixo, As Gurichas, Carballido, A Brixéria, Cospindo, Carracido, Cedeira, Ponteso, between others... I go though the bridge over the Allones river, and I keep following along the AC429 national road, not hitchhiking, just walking fast. And so, after having passed Sinde, Borneiro, As Pias, Reparada, Vimianzo, Vilaseco, Berdeogas, Bustelo, Lobelos, and Sardiñeiro de Abaixo, I reach the so colled lobster cove and then, finally, the Cape Finisterre, that ages ago was appointed as “the world’s end”, this is, it is here, at this rocky beach, that I end up meeting with some pilgrims coming from the many corners of Europe, and say, as I’m already approaching some of these people here around this fire, I realize what they are actually doing right now… this is, some of them are actually burning their socks, spreading the smoke and the smell around, laughing while doing it, and… as it goes, throwing these same burnt socks down the cliffs by the sea… Thus, while watching them, I wish I could do the same, but no, because, actually, I’m not wearing any socks… so, I have this idea, instead of socks, I end up burning my shoes, and then yes, like them, I’m throwing my burnt snikas down the cliffs by the sea… and so, in the meanwhile, after exchanging some words with a few of those pilgrims here wandering around the fire, I get to know that most of them are actually coming from Eastern Europe, but, not only that, there are also a couple of them coming from that countries on the strip of land between Europe and Asia, this is, the so-called middle-east, and well, after getting to know about the reasons that impelled them to come here, nothing religious, I may say, we all get into some kind of singing, and further… as I see some of them actually playing castanets while doing some dancing moves, I also start to rummage inside my rucksack, and from there picking my small harmonica that instantly I start to blow while actually washing my feet on the sea. And say, after much playing and dancing around this rugged rocks, some of us become acquainted, share stories, divide in small groups, and in a while, me and my group are already walking in the direction of Santiago de Compostela, a city about fifty miles from here, to the east… and so, once there, as we go through this clerical city, soon we get to understand how the locals are actually tired of all this shabby pilgrims coming here to spread their misery around, people in the search of miracles, others, just mere tourists, interested in photographing the misery of the others… and, as we get to the “plaza del Obradoiro”, the main plaza in front of the main cathedral, my escorts disappear, and I go to explore the city alone, this is, I get to hear some conversations from the locals, and also, I meet some other travelers, and again, I get to hear stories about how they actually got here, and in the meanwhile there I go, setting myself  under a porch, playing the harmonica, I mean, busking… this is, right now clusters of people are actually passing by in front of me, groping through the haze, some looking at me with indignation, this while the bells from the adjacent cathedrals clatter, as thus, as they clatter, I’m actually trying to play in their rhythm… this is, time passes by, and when night is already coming, I see two strange dudes getting close, one thinner, the other fatter, smiling and smirking, exchanging whispered comments between them while approaching... And so, at some point, the thinner one is already offering me loose wine, while the other, the chubbier one, just sits down on the floor on my side and begins ordering people to get closer and give money to the player (me). This is, in a while, they are both saying nonsense things in a pretentious semi-operatic tone, and eventually, at some point, the thinner one even starts doing some dancing steps, with one hand on the chest, and the other, the bustier one, here he is now, rolling on the floor at our front, tying up the passers-by, and laughing non-stop while doing so. And well, as it goes, the gaunt faced one is already giving me orders, telling me to play it slower and simpler, say, telling me to play only the bass notes, to do like a waltz rhythm, and, accordingly, as I do it, here he comes, already asking me pointless questions, and then singing with some kind of operatic style, well, not really operatic but… while the other, the chubbier one, that before was sitting on the floor, is now calling “Vaca Loca” to anyone that passes by our side, and then, immediately, offering the neck of his bottle to whoever deposits coins inside the hat at our front. And so, at this point, the gaunt faced one, is actually singing about “damas desnudas con bigotes de harina...”; “filipoyas místicos…”; “piruletas macabras…” and other things I can’t really understand, coz his language sounds like Russian. And then, just then, when the wine is finished and his voice begins to fail, I see them confiding something between themselves in my back, and so, as a result of this, in a while, I’m actually being invited to leave this place and accompany them somewhere, this is, they need a driver, the gaunt faced one tells me. And promptly, without knowing about directions, I accept to be their driver, thus, after collection the coins from that hat set on the floor here in front of us... there we go, already leaving this place, but, as we try to advance, the chubbier one doesn’t want to move, and then, when he tries to move, actually, he keeps going against walls and stuff, even falling on the floor a couple of times, this because he is dead drunk, so, both of us have to supporting him on the move, bracing him both sides, so he doesn't fall to the ground again. And thus, while we pull him, actually, he continues to snort words, things that are incomprehensible, this while his friend keeps pulling him, giving him shoves, offering him a beating, a scene that is somehow comic and depressing at the same time. And therefore, in those ways we wandering through the city, actually looking for the place they have parked their car… and, while advancing, the chubbier one, despite being almost in a sleeping mode, when he opens his eyes, he is still howling, calling dirty names to anyone that crosses our sight. And then, finally, when we manage to find the car, a Rover GSI, that actually was parked inside some public garden, a garden adjacent to some kind of semi-rotten church, we throw the paunchy one onto the back seat, and there we go, seating on the front, me on the driver’s seat, and the gaunt face, his name Alberto, on my side… this is, is not easy to maneuver the car out of this park, but when I manage to do it... following the hints of Alberto, I’m already getting on the AP-9, say, a motorway heading towards Pontevedra, and as it goes, with my co-pilot getting asleep, and the one in the back already snoring, after passing Vigo and Ó Porriño, I’m actually driving towards the Portuguese border, because those were the instructions Alberto gave me. And so, accordingly, as we pass the border, I have to wake him up again, because I need to know about directions… And so, as we pass Valença, the first town in Portuguese lands, Alberto (half asleep), order me new directions, and so, there we go, following along some national road and then an earthy path, and well, at some point, after having passed some pine tree forests, we are actually reaching some kind of farm with a few adjacent shacks, and at this point I understand, this place here is actually some kind blacksmith workshop, and so, following his instructions, I do park the car somewhere, and well, by now, as I try to get out of the car, instantly, I get surrounded by huge dogs that do not look very friendly, but, instantly, as its owner (Alberto) shouts at them, they back off. And so, at this point, as we make our way out of the car, leaving the paunchy one there snoring in the back seat… there we go, already getting inside some of the adjacent shacks, say, entering some kind of kitchen that looks more a box room, and, as we move around, the man just approaches some wood barrel, opens the tap and fills two glasses with that liquid, this is, “now you can drink, finally...” he says, then adding, “this is a different kind from the ones you may have tasted in Santiago, I mean, it’s home-made green wine… ‘maduro’ we say, green but mature… and so, after all this talking, I want to try it… and oh boy, it’s really good, not acid like the one I have tried in Spain... I mean, really fruity, and then I’m ready to leave this place… thus, after piercing through the scattered pieces of scrap metal and wood lying about the front-yard, I come back to the road, and, while imagining being pursued by a bunch angry dogs, I run all night, just stopping at the sun rise, by the entrance of some village, this is, here I’m, seated inside some bus-stop shed, and, I still have time to sleep a couple of hours, this before some kids arrive, kids that are actually coming to get on the bus that will take them to the school placed on bigger city in the surroundings… this is, Braga city, the third bigger city in this country in terms of population, they say. And so, as the bus comes by, I quickly move to the last seat, and, despite the cackling that circles me, I permit myself to sleep a bit more… just opening my eyes when we get to the last station, this is, the bus station at the city center… and so, as I get out of this station, and randomly follow some streets, watching the people, I end up in front of some kind of castle, at a colorful garden, with some kind of romantic fountain in the middle, and thus, by this fountain I rest for a while, but, it’s early, so, not much people are coming into this garden, just a couple of youngs are crossing it, from time to time, and then, at some point, a homeless guy actually approaches me and asks for a cigarette, and so, I give him a stone that I had in my pocket, and, while staring at this stone, he starts to tell me the story of “Santa Barbara”, the patron saint of this garden and the castle on our back, this is, he says that “...in Vila Real, a city about one hundred kilometers from here, to the east, there lived a rich and powerful man who wanted to arrange a marriage for his daughter, Barbara, but the many suitors that he would bring to her, she would refuse, and so, he locked her in the tower of a castle, thus, making her unable to meet anyone of her interest, and then, one day, suspecting that some her suitors were actually entering through some kind of window that she herself had ordered to be opened in the this tower, her father, he himself, tried to kill her, but at the exact point that he was about to do so, a lightning came down from the sky and incinerated the man, being for this reason now, Santa Barbara, the patron saint of heavy artillery members, firefighters and miners who place their faith in this saint to protect themselves from unexpected explosions…” he says, and then, after hearing this fantastic explanation, this same man just accompany me until the surroundings of the train station, from where the motorway going in the southern direction departs, and as it goes, I quickly get a ride with some guy driving a Fiat Punto, actually driving in the direction of Oporto city, that is the place where I wanna go, and, because he works at some kind of laboratory, all the way we speak about virus and viruses, starting by the Escherichia coli, “also known as E. Coli,  a gram-negative, facultative anaerobic, rod-shaped, coliform bacteria of the genus Escherichia that is commonly found in the lower intestine of warm-blooded organisms”, he says. And accordingly, about thirty minutes after, I’m already in Porto city, this is, at Boavista Square, some kind of roundabout on the north branch of the city... and so, as I ask directions people point me in a certain way, and soon I’m actually advancing through stone paved roads that lead me to the small Cedofeita church, a church with more than one thousand years, some locals say, and they also say that this church as actually some kind of municipality house from the Suebi, the Germanic people that I heard about in A Coruna. And then, after some small conversations about the Suebi and other Germanic tribes from that time, like the Marcomanni, the Quadi, the Hermunduri, the Semnones, and the Lombards, I go through the Cedofeita street, a pedestrian street that gives me the impression that I’m actually in Napoli, I don’t know why. And further, as I reach the main historic building from this city, the Clérigos Tower, a building with about three hundred years, that was a construction ordered by the “Clérigos Pobres Brotherhood”, a brotherhood that was a merger of three pre-existing brotherhoods that developed in the Santa Casa da Misericórdia do Porto, this is, the Brotherhood of São Pedro ad Vincula, the Congregation of São Filipe Néri and the Confraternity of Our Lady of Mercy. And so, I get to know, after the merger, the name of the brotherhood became “Confraria de Nossa Senhora da Misericórdia, São Pedro e São Filipe Néri”, later simplified as “Brotherhood of Clérigos”. And I also get to know that, the new brotherhood, intending to have its own headquarters, soon tried to achieve this objective, and when, in the beginning of the eighteenth century, they were offered land in the this so-called place of Cruz de Cassoa, next to the Adro dos Enforcados (a plot of land already outside the Fernandina Walls, near Olival, olive tree field, where criminals sentenced to hang and those who died outside of religion were buried), it was here, not without some controversy, that the house and Clérigos Tower would be built. And so, now, as I go down the Clérigos street, soon I reach the “praça da liberdade” or the “liberty square” at the bottom of “Aliados street” where is a monument to Dom Pedro IV, that at the same time as also Dom Pedro I, the first emperor of Brazil. And then, after turning right in front of the São Bento train station, I pass a series of terraces with skewed tables, and people sitting in a weird way, a place that, again, gives me the impression that I’m actually in Napoli, and continuing, as I go down a narrow pedestrian street called “Rua das Flores”, this is, “Flowers street”, instantly, some gypsy guys come to me offering cocaine and axixe, and, as I refuse it, one of guys even explains me that, the “tripas à moda do porto” dish is actually made from the muscle wall of a cow's stomach chambers, and “not from the intestines”, as some say, he says. And then, as I keep going down this “Rua das flores”, I appreciate the buildings with their tiled facades, some of them in semi-ruin, but still, with their lush pots of flowers up there, on the narrow verandas on the third or fifth floors. And then, after passing a couple of souvenir shops (actually owned by Indian dudes), I see, under some kind of porch, seated on the floor, a cadaveric man under a big umbrella,  talking bullshit to the passersby, this is, some kind of junkie, injecting his body in front of everybody, and so, I think to myself, definitely some kind of modern days Diogenes. And further, after leaving him alone, I pass some more buildings that look shutdown, but actually I see people getting in and out through that doors, and they are actually speaking foreign languages. And then, as I keep advancing, I come to approach this girl with an old fashioned bicycle on her side, the bicycle actually all covered with small drawings of paisajes, aquarelles, and so, at the first look, I get interested in one of her drawings, say, a drawing with a man in a trench coat, actually launching a large paper airplane into the air. And I also like his hat, coz, it looks like a postman from the old times. And, as I say this to her, straight away, she decides to offer me the drawing, and in exchange, I also offer her some stones I have in my pockets. And then, further, as I keep going down, I see a guy announcing lottery tickets, a woman selling crochet clothes, and then, as I pass a couple of restaurants with their tables in the middle of the street, and all the ones seated on these tables are tourists, and some more abandoned buildings on both sides of this street, buildings also covered with bluish mosaics, and on the ground floor, between the rusty pillars, there are some antique dealers, antique dealers that also sell costume jewelry, and then, as I get to the bottom of this street, I pass some kind of church with sea monsters coming out of its facade, and also, in front of the small entrance hall of this barricaded church, I see a brunette guy seated on the steps of this same church, not young not old, and, as I seat on his side, “my name is Fred”, he says, and when I ask him from where he’s from, “I’m Brazilian”, he says, and then, “but during the first years I lived in in this country, I lived in Lisbon, not here… but then… I traveled a bit through all western Europe… this is, I went to Spain, France, Italy and even Germany, where I stayed for a while, but that snow, man! That cold! I got depressed, I got sick, and in the end… it wasn't easy to come back. I mean, it wasn’t easy at all, but when I finally managed to do it, I ended up here, and so, I decided to make my base here, instead of Lisbon, which has already too many Brazilians…”, And, after hearing this, I also decide to say something about Berlin, but it looks that he’s not listening now, instead, he starts to hit the steps from the stairs where we are, this to show me that he is a drummer, and me, without wasting time, I also have something to show him, so yeah, there we go, both with the asses up and the arms down hammering this stony staircase with the palms, say, producing what can be called an impromptu drum battle. And, well, as it goes, after a while we are already being surrounded by a bunch of tourists and curious people taking photos of the situation, but then, we kick them out and move away. So, this is, as it goes, we move to Ribeira, really downtown, an area by the river, the Douro river, and so, on the way we buy a couple of wine bottles, and then, while we walk by the river, we pass some stalls with embroidered fabrics, handmade jewelry, etc. And just then, when we get close to that double decked bridge, the so-called “Don Luís” bridge, we go down by the water, and, as we go he actually presents me to some of his friends actually living here in barracks under the bridge... and so, in a while, we are already sharing drinks with them, and they, they also share some of their drinks with us, and then, there they go, inside their tents, then coming back with a bunch of percussive items like, djambês, timpanis, snare-drums, many kinds of tambourines, cymbals, pumpkin-shakers and other kinds of shakers, and so, there we go now, more and more close to the water, playing all this percussive stuff all night long. And so, just next morning I actually go across that bridge, say, when coming to the end of this bridge, I turn right, and while walking by the river on the other side, I actually pass by a bunch of Port wine cellars, this is, I pass brands like “Cockburn's”; “Taylor's”; “Cálem”; “Burmester”; “Sandeman”; “Ramos Pinto”; “Graham`s”; “Ferreira”; etc. And so, in the meantime, after having passed some ruins, a shipyard, some buildings under construction, and a series of abandoned lots, I’m actually by the sea, at the southern mouth of Douro river, in a place with some kind of dunes, and some bones buried there among the shards, and as it goes, the tide is actually rising and falling, quickly and then slowly, without rhythm, treacherous. And, as it goes, after reaching the Lavadores neighborhood, I go in search of the national road by the coast, going south, and accordingly, when I find it, there I stand at an intersection, showing up my thumb. And so, being taken by this and that car, I actually pass cities like Espinho, Esmoriz, Santa Maria da Feira, Ovar, Aveiro. Figueira da Foz, Nazaré, Peniche and Mafra, and well… soon I'm already going through the April’s bridge that goes over Tejo river, the river that separates Lisbon from Almada, or Al-ma'adan, “the mine”, and say, at this point, I’m actually being taken by a former university teacher, currently talking about Dona Urraca, apparently, the daughter of the first king of Portugal, he says, “Urraca was born in Coimbra in one thousand one hundred forty eight, and, she was the daughter of Afonso I, the first king of Portugal, and Maud of Savoy, the second or third daughter of Amadeus III, Count of Savoy and Maurienne, and Mahaut of Albon, the sister of Guigues IV of Albon, applied ‘le Dauphin’... and, one of her aunts, Adelaide of Maurienne, was actually the queen consort as the wife of King Louis VI of France, and one of her great-grand-uncles was Pope Callixtus II… and so, coming back to Dona Urraca, she actually married Ferdinand II of León, but, the marriage would be annulled about ten years after, coz, it was discovered, they were direct cousins, great-grandchildren of Alfonso VI of León and Castile…” and as he tells this things about the beginning of Portugal, and its connections with Spain, we actually pass towns like Laranjeiro, Corroios, Amora, Coina, Palmela, Marateca, Palma, Alcacer do Sal, “one of the most ancient cities in Europe, founded by Phoenician hairs, and apparently… it provided salt, salted fish, horses for export and food for the ships that traded with Cornwall, a ceremonial county in South West England… but, later, would be invaded by the Arabs, and it would become the capital of the of the Al-Kassr province…under the Umayyad rule of Damascus… this is, after an internal victory over Muwallad rebels in 888, a Moorish fleet transported troops from Alcácer to Oporto, to support Al-Mansur Ibn Abi Aamir, that culminated in the destruction of the sanctuary of Santiago de Compostela, in Galicia, northwest Spain..” he says. And so, as we keep talking about the time when the Arabs ruled over what is now Portugal and Spain, we pass Ervideira, Grandola, Santa Margarida da Serra, Roncão, Santiago do Cacem, Barbuda, and then, as we drive on the side of Sines, a coastal city on the Alentejo region, he just says, “This city holds an important oil refinery and… it is also the birthplace of Vasco da Gama,  the 1st Count of Vidigueira, a Portuguese explorer and nobleman that was, it is said, the first European to reach India by sea…”. And so, then, as I wander through the city, they tell me that this city hosts an important folk music festival, simply named, Festival de Musicas do Mundo de Sines, where already played names like Shemekia Copeland, Omar Sosa, Taraf de Haïdouks, Black Uhuru, Sly & Robbie, Hedningarna, Tinariwen, Sa Dingding, Kronos Quartet, The Skatalites, Lee "Scratch" Perry, Tom Zé, Femi Kuti, Hermeto Pascoal, Marc Ribot, Master Musicians of Jajouka, Señor Coconut, Trilok Gurtu, Toumani Diabaté, Rabih Abou-Khalil, Mahmoud Ahmed, Salif Keita, Gogol Bordello, Seun Kuti, Nortec Collective and Alamaailman Vasarat, etc. “Oh, the Master Musicians of Jajouka, that is great, I love them…” I say. And then, as they tell me that the best beaches in this country are actually between this city and Sagres, a city on the southwest tip of Portugal, this name tells me something, yes, I have seen it before a lot of times, because yes, Sagres is also the name of a famouse beer brand in this country… And so, as I go down the Costa Vicentina, I pass wonderful depopulated beaches with excavated cellars made inside schist-greywacke sedimentary kind of  rocks, and birds coming from Africa, like the swallow and the black stork, or Ciconia nigra, that, as I get to know, “all years travels between central African countries, like Burkina Faso, Niger, and south Portugal…” a fisherman tells me. And as it goes, after crossing several cliffs, walking up and down roads between beaches and pine forests with sandy terrains, at some point, I would eventually reach the southernmost part of the country, this is, Algarve, and so, as I go though it, I get to know that this name Al-Garbe, simply means “the west” in Arabic language, and so, at some point, when I’m crossing Albufeira, a city famous for being a hub of many English expats, I get in a van with a guy with a goatee and a ponytail, his name Yan. And soon, I got to know that he is actually transporter, this is, “I transport staff between south Portugal and south Spain and the opposite…” he says. And so, along the way, he would confide about his roots… “Say, actually I’m the son of an unscrupulous Englishman of lost whereabouts and a sketchy Greek woman, I mean… my childhood was spent in different islands of the Aegean Sea, where my parents met and lived for a while… inlands like Corfu, Milos, Nexus,  Amorgos, Ikaria, Rhodes, Lesbos, etc… this is, in these islands I had contact with the many fugitives from the Asian world, say Turks, Arabs, and other Middle Eastern creatures… and so, still young, I got into problems related with these acquaintances… and, at a certain point, my father sent me to an aunt in Italy, and then another one in France, but I hated France, so, I ended up with my paternal grandparents in Yorkshire, where I spent part of my adolescence… this is, I did some schooling there and then, I would found myself on the road again with a group of hippie bastards… this is, with them I went from Europe to Russia, and then from Kazakhstan to Uzbekistan, from Tajikistan to India, and then, we would hit Bangladesh, Myanmar, and finally Thailand… and so, in the meanwhile, my would friends leave, and I would move to Hong-Kong, where I would work for a while… and then, with the money I did there, I would take a flight to the States, this is, I traveled across America, I mean, I hitchhiked from Washington to Texas and Miami, and then, I even ended up living in the Caribbeans, for a while…” he says, as we pass the border, and then the coastal cities of Cadis, Mazagón, Matalascañas, and the Parque Nacional de Doñana, an area of marshes, shallow streams, and sand dunes in the delta where the Guadalquivir River flows into the Atlantic Ocean. And so, once we reach Gibraltar,  a city located at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula,  I even help him to unload some furniture here and there, and then, as he keeps his travel, there I stay, this is, in this enclaved British city, I discover a great tunnel perfect for busking, located really in the city center,  and so, during some days I would play my harmonica there, this while watching the tourists passing by, tourist from all europe and some from the Maghreb world also. And so, in the intervals of time between my playing and my moments of wandering, I would attend some morocco-style cafes, humble places that greatly differ from all the other British style kind of thing, where old Maghrebean men come to drink shay and smoke big cigarettes, this, while having their exalted conversations in Arab, Darija or Llanito, a form of Andalusian Spanish heavily laced with English and some arabesque expressions. And so, here I’m now, more precisely at “Roxy”, one of that places, this is, here I stay with Amin, and as it goes, say, while we smoke some pot, eventually, he decides to explain to me how he has actually crossed the Baḥr al-Maghrib,  this is, the Mediterranean sea, and so, here he goes now, already asserting that, “The first time we did it… we actually did it in a small dinghy made of inner tubes from truck wheels, you see, ‘kasdi’, and it happened that, the sea… actually dragged us to where we did not expect, and so, unintentionally, we ended up landing in south Portugal… this is, as we landed in Algarve, straight away my friends left to Spain, leaving me alone there… and so, in the meanwhile, I would go to Lisbon, where I would remain for some time, coz, I may say… I liked the Portuguese people, they are humbler than the Spanish, but… there aren't many work opportunities in that country, and so, after a while, I would leave the big city and go to work illegally in the extensive orange tree farms of southern Spain, mainly located around Valencia, say, a city that actually have ferries to the famous island of Ibiza, ‘kasdi’, and, attracted by this name… somehow, I managed to get into one of that ferrie, illegally, but, unfortunately or fortunately, I don’t know now, I got caught on the arrival and they sent me to a special kind of prison for illegals that turned out to be a forced labor camp, and so, there there was also people from Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and also some sub-sahariens, this is, people from Mali, Niger, Chad etc. And so, it was there that I learned how to properly speak and write is Spanish, and then, just then, when I already could speak and write in that language, they would send me back to Morocco… this is, my mother was happy to see me again, but I can’t say the same about my older brother, that soon would put me out of the house, this because, as he said, I had become an infidel... and so, I wandered through the country and eventually would end up in Ouarzazate, at the doors of the Sahara, on the side of the Barrage el Mansour Eddahbi, where I worked for a while, this before reaching Merzouga, a city on the border with Algeria… but you know, ‘kasdi’, in the desert there are no borders and so… after a while I would actually find myself in Tunis where I heard about a place people could cross into Europe, ‘kasdi’, and so... once again I got into a dinghy that would take me to Malta, a European island I had never heard about… say, an island where people speak Arab, Italian and French, all mixed up… and so, then, some months after I would actually reach Sicily, where I would for the Mafia, say, I would do numerous trips between Palermo and Napoli, and then, between Napoli and France, and so, that’s how I came to live in Montpelier and then in Marseille, but there, in Marseille, I got into a series of problems with some Algerian guys, this is, I got arrested, found illegal, and again, they sent back to my country… this is, my mother was happy to see me again, but not my brothers, the same as before… and so, after some months I would came back to Europe again, but, this time I would go to German, and then I would travel through some Balkan countries like Hungary, Serbia and Romania, and at some point, I would eventually reach Istanbul, in Turkey, this is, I would get some girlfriend there, and with her I would travel to Lebanon, where we separated, and then,  I would come back my country going all around the Baḥr al-Maghrib, this is, the Mediterranean sea, I mean, I would go through the occupied Palestinian territories, I would get a job in the port of Alexandria, in north Egypt, and so, after some time there, eventually, I would get in contact with the vessels transporting products between Egypt and other North African countries, and so… that’s how I managed to get back to my country...”, he says. And then, further, I'm no more in Gibraltar, this is, now I’m on the other side of the sea, in Tangier, more precisely, at the Grand Socco, a piazza at the top of one of the city's central hills, more precisely, an intersection of rue de la Plage with rue d'Italie with avenue Sidi Bou Arraquia with rue Sidi Bouabid with rue d'Angleterre and with rue de la Liberté, where there is a night market, and so, here I’m, now inspecting some old trinkets displayed on the cobbled floor around some kind of broken fountain, and so, as it goes, in the meanwhile, I even meet a group of young French people on their way to the Gnaowa music Festival, a festival taking place in the southern part of the country, more precisely Essaouira, former Mogador. Accordingly, I join the caravan, this is, I take the road with then in the direction of Essaouira, and so, going by the Atlantic coast, we pass Rabat, Casablanca, Safi, and then, I’m already at the camping area of the festival, in ‘Saouira, where I manage to make friendship with a couple of krakeb players, being the krakeb a large iron castanet-like thing that commands the rhythmic aspects of Gnawa music. And so, after some days there, attending jam sessions between Europeans, Arabs and Africans, roughly speaking, this people from the festival would take me to Agadir, and then to the Aglou Plage, that is already part of the Souss-Massa-Drâa... and then to Mirleft, perched on top of the gigantic ocher-colored cliffs, where I would eventually find locals selling pots of argan oil, and then Sidi Ifni and Tan-Tan, a town already surrounded by the desert and further, on the border with the Western Sahara, some guy driving a very old Mercedes Benz would actually take me to the  springs of the Layoun oasis, springs that furnish Laayoune, the capital of the western Sahara, and then, the driver of another truck with a load of pumpkins, would eventually give me a ride until the border with Mauritania... and afterwards, a group of Touaregs would actually take me to the vicinities of Dakar. And so, this is, here I’m now, at Malika beach, just on the side of some fish cottages where there are some pirogues turned upside down, pirogues with sentences saying things like “Papa Alada Ndao”; “Yeye Fatow”; “Dieng Dieng Dieng”; “Noo Ko Bokk”, etc. And then, as I wander around, a fisherman that is also a kora player, would eventually accompany me to the city center of Dakar, and so, this is, now, I’m already reaching the Boulevard Dial Diop, and then, as it goes, I pass the Place de l'Obélisque, I go down Boulevard du General de Gaulle that takes me to the Medina where I meet someone that actually wants buy my hair, and then, after passing the Our Lady of Victories monument, I go down Av. Pasteur, I pass the Ancien palais de Justice, now converted into an improvised art center, and finally, well, finally I arrive at Cap Manuel, a place that is said to be the westernmost point of Africa, and so, here I stay, just in front of the Atlantic sea, imagining what can be there, on the other side.

findings.title: Fifty places to paddle before you die : kayaking and rafting experts share the world's greatest destinations
findings.creator: Santella, Chris, author
description: 223 pages : 22 cm

In Fifty Places to Paddle Before You Die, the newest addition to the Fifty Places series, Chris Santella explores the best destinations for the diverse sport of paddling. The book features the world's top spots for kayaking, rafting, canoeing, and stand-up paddleboarding. Destinations include the Grand Canyon, Alaska's Kenai Peninsula, Baja California, Indonesia's Komodo Islands, and the Antarctic Peninsula, as recommended by paddling experts. Compelling travelogues are complemented by beautiful and vibrant photographs of the locations and travel tips to help readers experience the destinations for themselves

findings.description: Logbook of a whaling voyage to the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic Oceans in addition ot the Sea of Okhotsk, the Yellow Sea, and the Sea of Japan. Includes descriptions of whales and walruses seen or taken, illnesses, accidents, deaths at sea, interactions with natives, desertions, a rescue, and punishments. Also contains illustrations of whales, pen and ink drawings of the rigging, a drawing of a clipper ship, profile views, oil shipped home, accounts of provisions, and a crew list. A heavy gale damaged the windlass on September 1, 1861. On 4 September 1861, the vessel took two men from the ship Emily Morgan who had originally belonged to the bark Alice Frazier when lost. One whale caught on 23 March 1862 was eaten by sharks before the crew was able to cut in. A Japanese war steamer took possession of the Bonin Islands on 5 April 1862 but the Cicero encountered no problems. Isaac Wrisley assumed logkeeping duties on 13 November 1862 after William Chadwick (First Mate) was fired for incompetence. One man died of consumption on December 28, 1862. The vessel took on a passenger to Guam in February 1863. The vessel was damaged by ice on July 17, 1863. The keeper reported that the vessel was leaking on October 11, 1863. The vessel was damaged by a typhoon on October 16, 1863. On 4 June 1864, the vessel encountered several starving people on McKean Island (Kiribati) and gave them some supplies. A sperm whale stove a whaleboat on June 14, 1864. The vessel took a passenger off the brig Kohala to the Sandwich Islands in August 1864. One man was sick with rheumatism on October 13, 1864. John Rotch fell overboard on 29 January 1865 but was saved. The Steward died on April 14, 1865. Other places represented include Cape Verde, Marquesas Islands, Maui, Bonin Islands, Honolulu, Saipan, Guam, and Lahaina. Whaling grounds include the Cape Verde, Coast of Brazil, Falkland Islands, Coast of Chile, Tuamotos, Japan, On the Line, Japan Sea, Okhotsk Sea, and the Bering Sea grounds.; Old Dartmouth Historical Society (ODHS 18); Whaling vessel out of New Bedford, Mass., mastered by John R. Stivers, on voyage 9 October 1860 - 25 May 1865; managing agent, Loum Snow; built in Rochester, Mass., 1823.

findings.title: A stain in the blood : the remarkable voyage of Sir Kenelm Digby : pirate and poet, courtier and cook, king's servant and traitor's son
findings.creator: Moshenska, Joe, 1983- author
description: xix, 553 pages : 24 cm

On 16 August 1628, five battle-scarred English ships sailed through the narrow entrance of the harbour on the Greek island of Milos. Dropping anchor, the 25-year old captain banqueted with the local lord before sitting down to write an account of his journey - an account that would transform him entirely. Sir Kenelm Digby was known as one of the most extraordinary Englishmen who ever lived: a trusted advisor to the King, a pioneering philosopher and scientist, a friend and patron to Ben Jonson, Thomas Hobbes and van Dyck, and a thinker whose ideas are as relevant now as they were during his own troubled times. He was also widely known as the 'son of a traytor and husband of a whore': a man who witnessed his father's gruesome execution for high treason, and the lover of the most celebrated beauty of the age, Venetia Stanley. In an attempt to clear his name, and on a quest for personal glory, Digby assembled a fleet and set sail for the Mediterranean. His journey - encompassing fevers, mutiny, piracy, daring rescues and heroic sea battles - is a great and terribly overlooked adventure, and a prism through which to view England during one of the most pivotal periods in its history. A Stain in the Blood is the story of a remarkable life, and of a journey that helped to shape a nation. It is a revelatory first work of non-fiction by one of the brightest young writers and thinkers of today

findings.title: [Eagle (Ship) of Fairhaven, Mass., mastered by Samuel Perry, keeper Stephen Reed Delano, on voyage 18 December 1840 - 22 April 1843],
creator: Eagle (Ship : 1825-1846)
Delano, Stephen Reed
findings.description: Logbook of a whaling voyage to the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Includes descriptions of whales seen or taken, accidents, illnesses, desertions, punishments, and shipboard medicine. Also contains whale stamps, profile views, accounts, and a crew list. Three men were sick with scurvy on November 17, 1841. The ship landed at Maui and traded oil and flour for goats and pineapples on April 21, 1842. One man cut two of his toes off with a mincing knife on June 20, 1842. First mate Stephen R. Delano was left at Maui due to sickness on 26 August 1842, with the logbook being pooly kept as a result after this date. Whaling grounds include the Coast of Chile, Off Shore, Galapagos, On the Line, Coast of Brazil, and the 36/36 grounds.; Old Dartmouth Historical Society (ODHS 328); Whaling vessel out of Fairhaven, Mass., mastered by Samuel Perry, on voyage 18 December 1840 - 22 April 1843; managing agent, Hiram Henry Stackpole; built in Kennebunk, Maine.

Combe, William, 1741-1823. (editor)
Mackenzie, Roderick, d.1844. (author)
findings.description: Mackenzie, Alexander (Sir): 1763-1820. Born on island of Lewis; immigrated to New York then Montreal; entered service of Finlay, Gregory & Co., c. 1779; subsequently employed by Gregory, McLeod & Co. and NWC; in charge of Fort Chipewyan from 1788; retired to England, 1799; created knight bachelor, 1802; returned to Canada and fur trade, 1802-1808; cousin of Roderick Mackenzie (Wallace, Dictionary of Canadian biography ). // Combe, William: 1741-1823. Prolific English writer; assisted Alexander Mackenzie in preparation of Voyages , 1801 ( Dictionary of National Biography ). // Mackenzie, Roderick: d.1844. Fur trader; cousin of Sir Alexander Mackenzie; brother of Henry MacKenzie (Wallace, Dictionary of Canadian biography ). // After the preface there follow 132 pages on the history of the fur trade in the North West. Some authorities think this was written by his cousin, Roderick MacKenzie. According to the Dictionary of National Biography , Voyages , 1801, was compiled by William Combe from Mackenzie's notes. Includes vocabularies of the Knisteneaux, Algonquin, Chepewyan, Nagailer, and Atnah Indian languages. Errors in paging: page ix numbered xi; page 190 unnumbered; pages 212-216 numbered 214-218. Also published, 2nd edition, London: Printed for T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1801 ([2], cxxxii, viii, 412, [2]p.); including some material by Bougainville, London: Printed for T. Cadell, Jun. and W. Davies et al., 1802 (2 vols.); 1st American edition, New York: G.F. Hopkins, 1802 (viii [i.e. ix], 94, 296p.); 2nd American edition, Philadelphia: John Morgan, 1802 (viii, cxxvi, 392p.); 3rd American edition, New York: Evert Duyckinck, 1803 (viii, 437p.); edited by Richard Phillips and included in, A collection of voyages and travels, from the discovery of America to the commencement of the nineteeth [sic] century , vol.24, London: Printed for Richard Phillips, 1809 (392p.). New York: W.B. Gilley, 1814 (2 vols.); Toronto: George N. Morang, 1902 (2 vols.); with introduction by Robert Waite, New York: New Amsterdam Book Co., 1902 (2 vols.); New York: A.S. Barnes, 1903 (2 vols.); with introduction by W.L. Grant, Toronto: Courier Press, 1911 (2 vols.); New York: Allerton Book Co., 1922 (2 vols.), reprinted New York: AMS Press, 1973; with introduction by Charles William Colby and illustrations by C. Keith Gebhardt, Toronto: Radisson Society of Canada, 1927 (xxviii, 498p.); Ann Arbor, Mich.: University Microfilms, 1966 (cxxxii, viii, 412p.); [New York]: Readex Microprint Corp., 1966 (cxxxii, viii, 412p.); with introduction by Roy Daniells, Edmonton: M.G. Hurtig and Rutland, Vt.: Tuttle, 1971 (xx, cxxxii, 412p.). Also published as Alexander Mackenzie's voyage to the Pacific Ocean in 1793 , edited by Milo Milton Quaife, Chicago: Lakeside Press, 1931 (xxix, 384p.), reprinted, New York: Citadel Press, 1967 (xxix, 384p.). The 1789 journey also published in Exploring the Northwest Territory , edited by Ted Hayden McDonald, Norman: University of Oklahoma Press, [1966] (xiii, 133p.). The 1793 journey also published in First Man West: Alexander Mackenzie's journal of his voyage to the Pacific Coast of Canada in 1793 , edited by Walter Sheppe, Montreal: McGill University Press and Berkeley: University of California Press, 1962 (ix, 366p.), reprinted Westport Conn.: Greenwood Press, 1976 (ix, 366p.) and as Journal of the voyage to the Pacific , New York: Dover Publications, 1995 (ix, 366p.). Translated as Alexander Mackenzie's Esq. Reisen von Montreal durch Nordwestamerika nach dem Eismeer und der Sud-see in den Jahren 1789 und 1793: nebst einer Geschichte des Pelzhandels in Canada , Hamburg: B.G. Hoffmann, 1802 ([1], 1 leaf, [xiv], 585, [3]p.); translated by E.B. as Alexander Mackenzie's Esq. Reisen von Montreal durch Nordwestamerika nach dem Eismeer und der Sud-see in den Jahren 1789 und 1793? , Berlin: s.n., 1802 (408, [508]p.); translated and edited by Mathias Christian Sprengel as Alexander Mackenzie's Reise nach dem nördlichen Eisemeere vom 3. Jun bis 12. September 1798 , Weimar: Verlage des Landes-Industrie-Comptoirs, 1802 ([2], 61, [1]p.). For French version see Peel 54.

findings.title: Christophe Colomb (Enzo Biagi et Milo Manara, 1991)
findings.creator: Yaransu
findings.description: Le 3 août 1492, Christophe Colomb entame son fabuleux voyage. Ce n'est que bien plus tard qu'on se rendra compte qu'il n'a pas eu seulement pour résultat la découverte d'un nouveau continent mais qu'il a aussi marqué la fin d'une période de notre histoire. Une page est tournée. C'est la fin du Moyen Age. L'humanité a remporté une victoire sur les forces obscures de la nature. Les mers et les océans de notre planète apparaissent sur les cartes. La preuve que la terre est ronde est définitivement établie. Le commerce international peut donc se développer. Après 1492, les pays européens vont connaître un nouvel essor économique. Mais la vague de colonisation qui va suivre les découvertes de Colomb aura de nombreux côtés négatifs. L'Européen respecte très peu la culture des peuples qu'il rencontre. Pillages, massacres et dévastations en masse. La découverte des Amériques fut aussi le début d'une période de génocide et de soumission des plus barbares.

In a bid to reduce discontent over price hikes, the government has announced that it would double the subsidy on basic foodstuffs. None-theless, prices for basics will rise substantially. NOTES This is the first time in many years that the Chinese have fired live rounds at one of the offshore islands. 25X1 25X1 the Chinese do not seem to be in any position to threaten Kinmen Island, which has a large number of Nationalist troops in strong defensive positions. Peking doubtless also recognizes the dip-lomatic risks, especially with the US, that any attack on Nation-alist territory would entail. Gierek implicitly admitted that his regime had made a mistake and promised to consult extensively with workers on future price changes. He also said that on the basis of these discussions, the government would work out a "modified concep-tion" of the price changes that would be presented to the Polish people "in due time." If the party carries through on the promise of genuine and widespread consultations, it eventually may recoup some of its authority. Sudanese President Nu-mayri seems to have foiled another coup attempt by military elements. A consultative mechanism was estab-lished among ministries responsible for internal security matters. As a first step, the ministers agreed: --to increase the exchange of data on past incidents; --to trade information on tactics and training of internal security forces; --to exchange police personnel; --to facilitate direct police contacts for dealing with air-plane hijackings, nuclear secu-rity problems, and natural and accidental disasters. The mechanism was set up outside the EC treaty framework in part to meet French objections. Paris has opposed past EC Commission efforts to place cooperative undertakings--the protection of nuclear materials for example--on a Community basis, arguing they essentially involve police functions that fall outside the EC's jurisdiction. Forces loyal to Numayri had the situation under control in Khartoum yesterday and were conducting mop-ping-up operations in various parts of the capital, according to the US embassy. Rebel strength appears to have been centered in an armored unit on the outskirts of Khartoum. The 23rd of September Communist League recently has increased its terrorist activities and may stage isolated attacks to try to inter-fere with the elections. The government will be taking exten-sive security precautions. The small extremist organization has killed 20 policemen in Mexico City this year. The violence stemmed from demonstra-tions protesting the Israeli govern-ment's decision to raise taxes in the occupied territory. The demon-strations ended a period of uneasy calm that had prevailed in the West Bank for the past five weeks. findings.title: Życie na wyspach. Chorwacka współczesna proza insularna
findings.creator: Anna Boguska
findings.description: Oddana do rąk czytelników książka jest próbą opracowania znaczeń i funkcji, jakie w najnowszej chorwackiej prozie insularnej odgrywa wyspa, co więcej, próbą, która ma doprowadzić do zanegowania potocznego, trywialnego i wyłącznie turystycznego wyobrażenia o kraju. Przedmiotem opisu jest osiem współczesnych, tzn. powstałych w drugiej połowie XX i na początku XXI wieku, książek (powieści i zbiorów opowiadań), których akcja rozgrywa się na wybranych wyspach wschodniego wybrzeża Adriatyku. Autorka dokonuje oglądu wysp, stosując metodę badania symbolu, którą w tekście Symbol daje do myślenia z tomu Egzystencja i hermeneutyka zaproponował Paul Ricoeur. Podążając za ideą filozofa, wskazuje cztery symbole – pustynię, więzienie, teatr świata i ogród – poprzez które usiłuje przybliżyć symbol podstawowy. Każdy z tematów opracowuje na podstawie dwóch różnych książek, zarysowując dwie odmienne interpretacje pojęcia oraz odkrywając, z jakimi ludzkimi doświadczeniami wiąże się funkcjonowanie konkretnego obrazu. Life on Islands: Contemporary Croatian Insular Fiction:   This book is devoted to the study of meanings and functions of the island in contemporary Croatian insular fiction. It is also an attempt to encourage the rejection of simplistic, trivial, strictly tourist representation of the country. The study focuses on eight contemporary works of fiction (seven novels and one collection of short stories written between the 1950s and 2000s) set on the islands off the eastern coast of the Adriatic. They are analysed applying Paul Ricoeur’s method of exploring the symbol, as proposed in “The Symbol Gives Rise to Thought”, the concluding chapter of his volume The Symbolism of Evil. Following his idea, the author of this study indicates four symbols: the desert, the prison, the theatrum mundi and the garden, by means of which she tries to approach the main symbol: the island. She elaborates on each of them on the basis of two different books, proposing two diverse interpretations of the notion in focus and uncovering attendant human experience they convey.

findings.title: Archaeal and bacterial diversity in an arsenic-rich shallow-sea hydrothermal system undergoing phase separation.
creator: Price, Roy E.
Lesniewski, Ryan
Nitzsche, Katja S.
Meyerdierks, Anke
Saltikov, Chad
Pichler, Thomas
Amend, Jan P.
findings.description: This article is from Frontiers in Microbiology , volume 4 . Abstract Phase separation is a ubiquitous process in seafloor hydrothermal vents, creating a large range of salinities. Toxic elements (e.g., arsenic) partition into the vapor phase, and thus can be enriched in both high and low salinity fluids. However, investigations of microbial diversity at sites associated with phase separation are rare. We evaluated prokaryotic diversity in arsenic-rich shallow-sea vents off Milos Island (Greece) by comparative analysis of 16S rRNA clone sequences from two vent sites with similar pH and temperature but marked differences in salinity. Clone sequences were also obtained for aioA-like functional genes (AFGs). Bacteria in the surface sediments (0–1.5 cm) at the high salinity site consisted of mainly Epsilonproteobacteria (Arcobacter sp.), which transitioned to almost exclusively Firmicutes (Bacillus sp.) at ~10 cm depth. However, the low salinity site consisted of Bacteroidetes (Flavobacteria) in the surface and Epsilonproteobacteria (Arcobacter sp.) at ~10 cm depth. Archaea in the high salinity surface sediments were dominated by the orders Archaeoglobales and Thermococcales, transitioning to Thermoproteales and Desulfurococcales (Staphylothermus sp.) in the deeper sediments. In contrast, the low salinity site was dominated by Thermoplasmatales in the surface and Thermoproteales at depth. Similarities in gas and redox chemistry suggest that salinity and/or arsenic concentrations may select for microbial communities that can tolerate these parameters. Many of the archaeal 16S rRNA sequences contained inserts, possibly introns, including members of the Euryarchaeota. Clones containing AFGs affiliated with either Alpha- or Betaproteobacteria, although most were only distantly related to published representatives. Most clones (89%) originated from the deeper layer of the low salinity, highest arsenic site. This is the only sample with overlap in 16S rRNA data, suggesting arsenotrophy as an important metabolism in similar environments.

findings.title: Wish you were here
findings.creator: Connelly, Victoria, author
description: 391 pages (large print) ; 24 cm

Sun, sea and secrets. A week on the sunny Greek island of Kethos is just what Alice Archer needs, even if she has to put up with her difficult sister. Stella's tantrums are a fair price to pay for crystal-clear waters, blue skies and white clifftop villas. When Alice meets Milo, a handsome gardener at the Villa Argenti, for the first time she suddenly feels beautiful, alluring and confident. But is it just holiday magic or will the irresistible pull between Alice and Milo survive against all odds?
Published by W.F. Howes Ltd under the Clipper imprint

findings.description: The past four years have witnessed an unexpected warming of relations between the United States and China. The rancor generated by the EP-3 spy-plane controversy and the debate over American arms sales to Taiwan dissipated in the wake of the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks on New York and Washington. Beijing supported the U.S.-led campaign in Afghanistan. It has cooperated with the United States in the war on terror, sharing intelligence and coordinating law-enforcement efforts. Perhaps most strikingly, Chinese officials have worked quietly but assiduously to break the nuclear impasse on the Korean Peninsula. Understandably, many observers in the West have hailed the seeming shift in Chinese foreign policy in a more pro-American direction, interpreting it as evidence that Sino-American relations will remain on the upswing. Other moves by Beijing, however, cast doubt on this optimistic view. Wary of Taiwan s seeming drift toward independence, China has stationed some five hundred ballistic missiles across the Taiwan Strait from the island and is deploying additional missiles each year. These missiles have no plausible purpose other than to coerce Taipei into opening talks on reunification with the mainland or, failing that, to batter the island into submission.

THE COMMUNIST SCENE (19 April - 23 May 1969) June 1969 I. Husak's First Month in Czechoslovakia II. On the Eve of the World Communist Conference III. Strange Bedmates in the Balkans IV. Briefly Noted: A. Chinese Policy after the Ninth Congress B. Soviets Meddle in Finnish Communist Affairs C. Lenin Centennial I. One Month of the New Husak Regime in Czechoslovakia On 17 April, with the second Soviet intervention, Gustav Husak became Secretary General of the Czechoslovak Communist Party (CSCP) and thus top ruler in Czechoslovakia, taking orders from no one except the Soviets. His reign of something more than a month has been marked by definite steps toward Soviet-style "normalization" of the country's situation, which for the past year has been characterized by the Soviets as a "crisis" situation because it did not conform to the pattern of rule practiced in the Soviet Union and its other Satellites. Husak has proceeded in several directions simultaneously in his effort to satisfy the Soviets. Prospects are that he may restore Czechoslovakia to passive Communist orthodoxy using little noticeable violent suppression or old- fashioned Stalinist methods, in fact much less than there was reason to fear at first. Among Husak's moves are the suspension of some of the more out- spokenly liberal newspapers and magazines, including the Studentske Listy, Politika,(a major organ of the Central Committee of his own Communist Party), Listy, Reporter and others. Other publications that do not actively support the party line or are critical of the Soviet Union can expect to suffer a similar fate. On some newspapers, such as the CSCP daily, Rude Pravo, he has installed a new staff of editors he is sure will propagate his line. Some observers have noted that Husak is also substituting "reliable" Communists in place of liberals throughout the party and government hierarchy as an important measure to insure that his orders will be closely followed. There have been sporadic unrest and occasional demonstrations by various elements of the population, as on May Day, on the eve of 6 May (anniversary of the entry of U.S. troops into Western Czechoslovakia during World War II), and again on official Liberation Day, 9 May. In each case, Husak has ordered swift measures to cope with the possibility of mass anti-Soviet, anti-regime demonstra- tions by having the police round up and arrest as many thousands of demonstra- tors as necessary. Thus far, even though an estimated 5,000 students and workers demonstrated at Plzen (Pilsen) on 5 May, none of the popular resentment has gotten out of control, as far as is known. Approved For Release 2000/08/29 : CIA-RDP79-01194AO00500100001-0 Approved For Release 2000/08/29 : CIA-RDP79-01194A000500100001-0 Thus Husak has moved decisively to demonstrate to his Soviet masters that he intends to fulfill their explicit or unspoken requirements. He has supported all Soviet foreign policy initiatives, especially doing what he can to assure that Czechoslovakia will not become a bone of contention during the World Communist Conference. His most servile move was to make a speech in Moscow on May Day in which he all but accepted the Soviet version of the pre-invasion situation in Czechoslovakia, (i.ea, that a counterrevolution was imminent), and therefore, in effect, seemed to agree that the Soviet-Warsaw Pact invasion was justified. This, all previous CSCP leaders had refused to do. The Husak speech was promptly featured in Pravda, but this sensitive portion was omitted in the version published for the Czechoslovak public. Seemingly as a reward for Husak's good behavior, the Soviets quietly suspended publication and distribution of their illegal Czech-language newspaper Zpr.avy, hated by the Czechs as a brazen symbol of Soviet rule. Husak may hope that the Soviets will further reward him by removing some Soviet troops from Czech soil or possibly by granting a hard. currency loan, which the Czech economy sorely needs in order to buy modern western equipment and help make the Czechs competitive in world trade. Some observers believe that the enigmatic Husak personality hides a strong will, a sense of independence, and a fierce sense of nationalism which make him not altogether to the Soviets' liking, But thus far, for all practical purposes, he has shown less independence than his predecessor Alexander Dubcek, despite extreme pressures kept to his commitment to preserve the important freedoms of speech, assembly and press. II. At Issue On the Eye of the World Communist Conference Czechoslovakia has been the main cause of the considerable disarray in the world Communist movement, and at the forefront of criticism of the Soviet Union has been the Italian Communist Party (PCI). The PCI has been critical both of the military intervention and of the Soviet-inspired effort to snuff out the Dubcek-led experiment in a humanistic and progressive Communism. Buts now that a native Czechoslovak is taking the lead in accomplishing Soviet objectives in Czechoslovakia, the PCI has less reason to point an accusing finger at the real culprit: the CPSU. Nevertheless, the invasion of Czechoslovakia and its justification in the Brezhnev Doctrine of limited sovereignty gave added strength to pre- existing centrifugal forces that now threaten to throw more fragments of parties, if now whole CP's, out of the Soviet gravitational field. The period between the 23 May Preparatory Commission meeting and the end of the full- scale World Communist Conference, which starts 5 June, will witness a struggle between the centrifugal and centripetal forces in the movement. The Soviets will use every device their ingenuity can invent: pressure, persuasion, black- mail, bribery, to restore their centralized authority and control. If they do not succeed during this period in establishing some kind of international organization (as a latter-day variation of the Comintern or Cominform), they Approved For Release 2000/08/29 : CIA-RDP79-01194A000500100001-0 Approved For Release 2000/08/29 : CIA-RDP79-01194A000500100001-0 are certain to continue this effort after the conference. Centrifugal forces, foremost among them the PCI, but including also such parties as the Rumanian and the British, will oppose this Soviet aim and will try to gain acceptance of their principle of true autonomy for each party. What sort of equilibrium between these two forces will emerge from the Conference may become evident from the wording of the document that is finally adopted by the 60-odd parties expected to attend. The critical portion will concern the relations between parties, i.e., between the CPSU on the one hand and individual parties on the other. Reportedly this section is causing serious difficulty for the drafters. If the Soviets succeed in their effort, the document should show strong emphasis on the unity of the movement and the "duty" and "responsibility" of fraternal parties to "proletarian inter- nationalism" with a secondary role accorded the principles of autonomy and independence of parties. It might even include a statement suggesting or implying the desirability of some kind of formal international organization. If the independent-minded parties are able to persist in their views (their ultimate weapon being a refusal to sign the final document), it should be reflected in a corresponding dilution of the importance of unity, duties, and responsibilities, and a strengthening of the theme of party autonomy. III. Albania, Yugoslavia, Rumania, China --- Strange Bedmates Ever since the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia, the Rumanians, Yugoslavs, and Albanians have feared that the Soviets would apply the Brezhnev Doctrine to their countries and move against them militarily. For those far removed geographically or psychologically from the danger of Soviet invasion, it is easy to dismiss such fears as far-fetched or even as being self-serving propaganda, but it should be remembered that it was just such "detached" observers who, before the Czech invasion, believed that the deviations repre- sented by Czechoslovakia were not sufficient cause for the Soviets' taking such drastic action. Recently, Soviet attitudes toward Albania raised these Balkan countries' apprehensions to a new level. The authoritative CPSU journal Kommunist (No. 5, 26 March 1969) claimed that the Chinese had established military bases in Albania with the intention of installing missiles there. The Albanians re- jected these accusations (as did their long-time enemies, the Yugoslavs) but saw in them Soviet establishment of a pretext for military action against Albania. They were especially apprehensive inasmuch as they had formally withdrawn from the Warsaw Pact in September 1968 without subsequent Soviet recognition or acknowledgment of this fact. (Hungarian withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact was one main reason for the Soviet invasion of Communist Hungary in 1956.) The depth of Albanian concern is illustrated by the curious phenomenon of the Albanians' offering to make common cause with their archenemies, the Yugoslavs, in defense against a possible Soviet invasion. This position was made clear in an editorial 11 April in the main Albanian CP paper, Zeri i Popullit. The Yugoslavs, in turn, while suggesting that some Albanian views Approved For Release 2000/08/29 : CIA-RDP79-01194A000500100001-0 Approved For Release 2000/08/29 : CIA-RDP79-01194A000500100001-0 might be exaggerated, acknowledged that there was reason for concern since the Soviet accusation was false and therefore could quite logically be regarded as a trumped-up justification for military action. A military move against Albania would inevitably involve Yugoslavia, which has for months actively prepared its citizenry to resist Soviet invasion. The Albanians at the same time asserted, less surprisingly, that their fate is also linked to that of Rumania. Rumania has long been aware that, because of their relative independence of, and often outright opposition to, the Soviets, they could be the next victim of the Brezhnev Doctrine. In addition to this common fear, the two countries are bound by their mutual sympathy for Communist China, though for different reasons and in different degree. The Rumanians have discreetly supported the Chinese ever since the latter challenged Soviet claims to dictate the international Communist line, because the Rumanians themselves aspired to just such independence. The Albanians in their dispute with the Soviets found a willing ally in the Chinese and have been as vituperatively anti-Soviet as the Chinese themselves. The Chinese took until 7 May to register their view of the Albanian offer to make common cause with Yugoslavia and Rumania. China was able to acknowledge the logic of Albania's appeal to Rumania but unable to say a kind word about Yugoslavia, that archetype of revisionism. So the Chinese simply ignored the Yugpslav role. This spectacle of tangled Communist international relations clearly has its ludicrous aspects, but two serious lessons of import emerge. There can be no doubt that the three deviating Communist countries -- Albania, Rumania, and Yugoslavia -- despite important dissimilarities, feel threatened by the Soviet Union as a result of the invasion of Czechoslovakia. And despite the incredulity with which many may view these fears, they simply cannot be ignored, any more than the prospect of Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia should have been underestimated before 21 August 1968. Secondly, the mutually independent stance of all three countries vis-A-vis the Soviet Union is clear evidence of the potency of nationalism, even in the Communist world. This nationalism is one more proof of the falsity of the Communist myth, invented by Marx and enshrined by Lenin, that Communists as the vanguard of the working class regard "proletarian. internationalism" as a greater principle than looking after the national interest (traditionally contemptuously referred to by the Communists as "bourgeois nationalism"). IV. Briefly Noted A. Chinese CP Congress and National Policy As the dust settles after the long Chinese Communist Party Congress (1 - 28 April), it is evident that it was inconclusive. The length of the congress, particularly the time it took to put together a new Central Committee, is one of many tenuous indications suggesting a hard fight took place, with Approved For Release 2000/08/29 : CIA-RDP79-01194A000500100001-0 Approved For Release 2000/08/29 : CIA-RDP79-01194A000500100001-0 tough bargaining and pulling and tugging between two factions in the party. On the one hand there are the moderates, pragmatists, who want to come to practical grips with economic and diplomatic realities and whose leader is generally thought to be Chou En-lai. On the other hand, there are the fanatic, purist revolutionaries, to whom the Cultural Revolution and Mao Tse-tung's ideology, bound in a little red book, are the ultimate reality and an end in themselves. The congress and its aftermath suggest that both factions continue to have influence on Mao and his heir, Lin Piao, who are the final arbiters over policy proposals put forth by each faction. It would appear that Mao sometimes decides in favor of one group and policy and then reverses himself under the persuasions of the opposing group, so that policies can veer wildly and change tack even from day to day. This factional struggle may explain why the Chinese proposal last November to resume the Warsaw talks with the U.S. (initiated by the moderates) was abruptly cancelled the following February (by the fanatics). Factionalism, presided over by an aging and capricious Mao, could also explain the simultaneous pursuit of contradictory courses, for example the current Chinese agreement to talk with the Soviets about navigation problems along common border rivers while renewed armed clashes go on. B. Continued Soviet Intervention in Finnish CP Affairs In early April Soviet Politburo member Arvid Pelshe tried to mediate the dispute between the dominant moderate faction of the Finnish Communist Party and the Stalinist faction, which walked out of the 15th Party Congress (3-6 April) with the intention of forming its own Communist party. On 21 April Alexey Belyakov, chief of the Scandinavian Bureau of the CPSU Central Committee, quietly slipped into Helsinki to continue the Soviet pressure to prevent either side from perpetrating an organizational split in the Party. Thus far, Belyakov has been successful in that he has persuaded the two factions to sit down together and try to find common ground. As of mid-May, the two factions have not reached agreement and are continuing talks, not very optimistically. Helsinki newspapers suggest that the Stalinists themselves may split into one group that favors rejoining the regular party as an opposition faction and another group which will go ahead and form a separate party. C. Lenin Centennial The 100th anniversary of Lenin's birth falls on 22 April 1970. One of the major items to be discussed at the World Communist Conference 5 June will be the celebration of this centennial, which promises to take on vast proportions. Lenin's 99th anniversary this year was marked by a dull, un- inspired address by CPSU Secretary Ivan Kapitonov. More interestingly, Pablo Neruda, well-known Latin American Communist, launched his own celebra- tion in Santiago, Chile, with a flurry of newspaper features on various aspects of Lenin's life and work. He has promised to celebrate this god of the Communist world for the whole year. He has already embarked on a declared policy of appcasini. and flattering the Russians as the esscn tial prerequisite for the solution of all other outstanding problems. TT (TTT V June 1969 As a May Day rememberance for 1969, Walter Ulbricht's East German regime was rewarded with a long sought-after prize: cognizance by some non-Communist states of the German Democratic Republic's official exist- ence. Plans to grant diplomatic recognition to East Germany were announced on 30 April by the Government of Iraq and, eight days later, by the Government of Cambodia. At his first press conference held after the 25 May military coup which brought him to power, Sudan's new Premier Awadallah announced his government's intention to emulate Iraq. Ulbricht has long been convinced that just one non-Communist commit- ment would start a chain reaction throughout the Arab, African., and Asian worlds inspiring country after country to scramble onto a bandwagon labeled "GDR sovereignty." The East German regime already is recognized in all but name by many Third World countries through reciprocal trade missions or full-blown consulates. Now it is Ulbricht's ambition that these relationships be dignified by the highest sounding title in time for the East German 20th anniversary celebrations in October 1969 and presumably he believes that recognition thrice in a month will give his scheme the impetus it badly needs. Stepped up efforts to gain official status throughout the Third World can be expected within the next few weeks despite two great stumbling blocks, one military and the other economic, both of which portend a miscarriage of Ulbricht's ambition. May Day Rememberances The Iraqi, Cambodian, and Sudanese diplomatic acceptances of East Germany are matters of vested interest -- born not out of respect for "GDR sovereignty" but out of need to pay for past and probably promised future East German support on ticklish national or international issues. Of at least equal importance is the intense pressure the Soviet Union has exerted on these countries on behalf of East Germany, the leverage for which comes from years of intense cultivation and considerable economic and military aid programs. Iraq, for instance, received advanced-type Soviet MIG fighters well before Egypt. Moscow certainly has a very active interest in securing legitimization outside of the Communist Bloc for the "state" it created in East Germany. East German backing for almost every Arab cause sometimes exceeds even Moscow's pro-Arab endorsements -- particularly with regard to the Palestinian Arabs. The Iraqis specifically cited East German "support for the Palestinian peoples' just struggle to liberate their usurped homelands" as a reason for bestowing diplomatic recognition. Iraqi gratitude was reflected in Radio Baghdad's statement that,East Germany's "noble attitude toward our national issues" was just another reason for extending recognition.. Cambodia's diplomatic obeisance is another sign of extreme national sensitivity about the lack of world acknowledgment of Cambodian borders. Statements issued in both Pankow and Phnom Penh suggest that the new diplomatic ties are a belated reward to East Germany for her long- standing recognition of the border delineations most acceptable to Cambodia. On 5 May, Sheikh Ali Abdel Rahman, Sudan's leftist Foreign Minister and Deputy Premier, held a press conference at which he said he had recommended to the Sudanese Cabinet that Sudan follow in Iraq's footsteps in recognizing the German Democratic Republic because it was a "friendly country with honorable attitudes toward Arab causes." At that time, the suggestion was intepreted as designed to counteract a movement in the Sudanese Constituent Assembly to reestablish relations with West Germany and the U.S.A. However, the 25 May military coup which overthrew President Ismail el Azhari also thrust radicalism into a much more powerful position in Sudan. The new Prime Minister Babiker Awadalla held his first press conference two days later and announced that his government's first act of foreign policy would be to recognize East Germany because of "the East Berlin regime's opposition to Israel." A May Day Blunder While Moscow and all the other members of the Warsaw Pact this year eschewed their annual spring show of military prowess, Walter Ulbricht celebrated the day with loud and, enthusiastic saber-rattling throughout East Germany. Speeches by military leaders and four parades featuring missiles, tanks, and heavy artillery marked May Day in East Berlin as dedicated to "20 years of socialist military policy." This is the facet of Walter Ulbricht that must be understood by anyone toying with the acceptance of "GDR sovereignty': he remains the ever-ready hangman and executor for the Warsaw Pact, for the Brezhnev Doctrine -- the true "Stalinist" of Central Europe. May Day 1969 in East Berlin rekindled mew-cries of 21 August 1968 when Ulbricht's troops, mercenaries of the Soviet Union, were among those forces that moved into and occupied the sovereign state of Czechoslovakia. Warsaw Pact utilization of German troops, permitting them to march into a neighboring country, above all one previously occupied by Nazi Germany, was a flagrant violation of the Potsdam Agree- ment. Even the USSR, in August 1968, soon saw the grave error of sanctioning GDR military presence in occupied Czechoslovakia: all the wind went out of Soviet propaganda which was trying to portray the West Germans as the "aggressors plotting invasion."
